profile.purpose: A travel documentary episode of the Kenji Eats Japan series following Kenji's trip to Tsubame-Sanjō, Niigata, with his knife-making partners to visit Aiba Steel. It covers sourcing Japanese steel for his knife, how san mai steel works, the town's metalworking history and industry, and the local food and hospitality.
profile.thesis: Seeing Sanjō's centuries-old, highly specialized metalworking industry first-hand, through the Aiba family's steel business, changes how Kenji thinks about where knives come from. A new Aiba steel may make its way into his knives.
key_takeaways: Kenji and knife maker Gordon (Vonhelmick) were running low on high-quality Japanese steel for their handmade Shi-Toku knife, which led them to the Aiba family.
The Shi-Toku is a santoku with a curved tip that allows Western-style rock chopping.
Aiba has been in the metal business in Sanjō since 1861 and has a new steel coming that is the first approved for cutlery from the company in about three decades. Barbers already use it for scissors.
San mai (three-layer) steel puts a hard, high-carbon core between tougher outer layers to balance edge retention against brittleness. Kenji compares it to rebar in concrete.
Metalworking came to Tsubame-Sanjō about 400 years ago as a second industry to protect farmers from flood losses, rather than from out-of-work swordsmiths.
Sanjō factories and workers are highly specialized. Kenji contrasts the town's survival with Johnstown, Pennsylvania, and Bethlehem Steel, where his grandfather worked.
Less than 10% of Aiba's business is cutlery. Much of it is heavy machinery and specialty steel processing.
Niigata food highlights include multi-course onsen meals, aged snow beef, tempura fried tableside, and Sanjō's curry ramen.

outline.title: Introduction to new steel
outline.summary: Cold open teasing a new cutlery steel. Kenji explains that chefs are nerdy about knife details and that there is no single best knife.

outline.title: The quest for quality metal
outline.summary: Why the team went to Tsubame-Sanjō with knife-making partner Gordon. The Shi-Toku knife's design is described, along with the shortage of high-quality Japanese steel.

outline.title: Meeting the Aiba family
outline.summary: How a friend, Eugene, connected them with the Aiba family, steel merchants in Sanjō since 1861. The Aibas flew to Oregon and Seattle to meet in person.

outline.title: Properties of specialty steel
outline.summary: The upcoming Aiba steel, already favored by barbers for scissors, is extremely sharp, hard and tough.

outline.title: Understanding san mai steel
outline.summary: Explains three-layer san mai construction, the hardness versus brittleness tradeoff, the rebar analogy and tensile strength, and Kenji's 67-layer factory-made knife.

outline.title: The industrial history of Sanjō
outline.summary: Signs of metalworking around town, and the myth that knife makers descend from swordsmiths. Metalworking was introduced to Niigata's flood-prone farming region in the 17th century.

outline.title: Specialization in manufacturing
outline.summary: Sanjō moved from nails and farm tools to scissors and grooming tools. Factories and workers are highly specialized, which Kenji links to the quality of Japanese cutlery. Includes a Patreon thank-you.

outline.title: Global steel industry contrast
outline.summary: Kenji's grandfather worked at Bethlehem Steel in Johnstown, PA, an industry that didn't survive globalization. He contrasts this with Sanjō's niche specialty work.

outline.title: Factory scale and production
outline.summary: A blacksmithing dojo and a daikon-cutting record holder, then the huge scale of the Aiba factory: giant anvils, cast iron pouring and knife hammering, plus the town's metal museums.

outline.title: Hospitality and local cuisine
outline.summary: Onsen stays and multi-course seasonal Niigata meals, including snow beef and tableside tempura. Sanjō's specialty curry ramen is compared with curry udon.

outline.title: Innovation and conclusion
outline.summary: Kenji reflects on how seeing the process changed his view of knives. The Aibas keep innovating, and their steel may end up in his future knives.
